humanities_role_explanation: The items are expert-coded historical facts (presence/absence/inferred status of social, religious, legal and military variables across 600+ polities) from the Seshat Global History Databank. They test graduate/expert-level history knowledge itself, not a generic skill on humanities text.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text-only. Each item is a templated multiple-choice question naming a variable, a polity and a date range, with four answer options.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Models judge whether a historical characteristic (e.g. writing, fasting, battle axes) was present, absent, inferred present or inferred absent for a polity and time frame. This is expert-level factual knowledge of global history, plus a distinction between evidenced and inferred facts, in a 4-choice format and a 2-choice present/absent variant.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped to a single domain (global history knowledge) and a single question template derived from Seshat.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o, Llama-3-70B, Llama-3.1-70B (FP8), Llama-3.1-8B (FP8), Gemini-1.5-flash.

quantitative_metrics.note: Balanced accuracy and adjusted balanced accuracy (4-choice and 2-choice), with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

published_after_march_2023.note: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks track; evaluations run in August 2024.

summary: The paper introduces HiST-LLM, a benchmark built from the Seshat Global History Databank by converting 36,000 expert-coded data points on 600+ polities into multiple-choice questions. Seven LLMs are evaluated in a few-shot chain-of-thought setting. Performance is above chance but well short of expert knowledge, and it is better for earlier periods and uneven across regions.
key_findings: 4-choice balanced accuracy ranges from 33.6% (Llama-3.1-8B) to 46.0% (GPT-4-Turbo), against 25% for random guessing. 2-choice balanced accuracy ranges from 57.6% to 63.2% (GPT-4o best). Accuracy declines for more recent periods. Performance is best for the Americas and lowest for Oceania and Sub-Saharan Africa.
evaluation_unit: Seshat data point converted into a multiple-choice question
gold_upstream: Seshat Global History Databank (Turchin et al. 2015; Francois et al. 2016; Turchin et al. 2018). Per this paper, graduate-level research assistants coded the data under the supervision of established scholars, and 14,000 of 36,000 points were additionally expert-reviewed.
facets_explanation: Reference answers are the Seshat codes (Present, Absent, Inferred Present, Inferred Absent). They were coded by graduate research assistants under the supervision of professors and PhD-level researchers, with expert review for 14,000 of the 36,000 points. The question stimulus contains no evidence, so answering requires external historical knowledge. Scoring is exact match against a single code, and the paper does not treat annotator disagreement as a signal.
results_explanation: The abstract reports balanced accuracy 'ranging from 33.6% (Llama-3.1-8B) to 46% (GPT-4-Turbo)' in the 4-choice format. The headline score is therefore 46.0 balanced accuracy, which is mapped to the 'accuracy' label. The 2-choice variant on the same items gives 57.6 to 63.2. The largest gap I derived is Llama-3.1-8B, 57.6 (2-choice) vs 33.6 (4-choice), i.e. 24 points; the chance levels differ (50% vs 25%). The text in Section 5 states GPT-4-Turbo at 43.8%, which conflicts with Table 1's 46.0. No human baseline is reported. The regional asymmetry is stated as lowest in Oceania and Sub-Saharan Africa.
